overview.title: Reshaping and transposition; vectors as points and arrows
overview.chapter: 2 The mathematical building blocks of neural networks
overview.section: 2.3 The gears of neural networks: Tensor operations
overview.main_topic: The definition of tensor reshaping with a (3, 2) → (6, 1) → (2, 3) example, transposition as a special case, and the start of the geometric interpretation: a 2-D vector is a point (or an arrow from the origin) and vector addition chains arrows.
overview.central_idea: Reshaping rearranges a tensor's coefficients into a new shape without changing their number; transposition swaps rows and columns. Because tensor contents are coordinates of points, every tensor operation has a geometric meaning — addition, for instance, moves a point by a vector.
overview.importance: Reshaping and transposition are everyday operations for matching data to layers. The geometric view introduced here is the lens through which the book explains what neural networks do: chains of geometric transformations (p.62).
learning_objectives: Define reshaping and state its invariant (same total number of coefficients).
Trace the example (3, 2) → (6, 1) → (2, 3) and predict the coefficient order.
Define transposition as x[i, :] becoming x[:, i], and predict the shape of np.transpose of a (300, 20) matrix.
Explain why tensor operations have a geometric interpretation.
Picture A = [0.5, 1] as a point and as an arrow, and A + B with B = [1, 0.25] as chained arrows.
prerequisites: Introduction of tensor reshaping and the MNIST reshape (p.58)
Tensor slicing x[i, :] and x[:, i] (p.49)

summary:
**Reshaping defined.** Reshaping a tensor means rearranging its rows and columns to match a target shape; naturally the reshaped tensor has the same total number of coefficients as the original. The example starts with `x = np.array([[0., 1.], [2., 3.], [4., 5.]])` of shape `(3, 2)`. `x.reshape((6, 1))` produces a single column `[[0.], [1.], [2.], [3.], [4.], [5.]]` — the six values read off row by row. `x.reshape((2, 3))` then gives `[[0., 1., 2.], [3., 4., 5.]]`: the same six values, refilled three per row. In every case the count is 6.

**Transposition.** A commonly encountered special case of reshaping is *transposition*: exchanging the rows and columns of a matrix, so that `x[i, :]` becomes `x[:, i]`. With `x = np.zeros((300, 20))`, `np.transpose(x)` has shape `(20, 300)`.

**2.3.5 Geometric interpretation of tensor operations.** Because the contents of tensors can be interpreted as coordinates of points in some geometric space, *all* tensor operations have a geometric interpretation. Addition is the first example. The vector `A = [0.5, 1]` is a point in 2-D space (figure 2.6), commonly pictured as an arrow from the origin to the point (figure 2.7). Adding a second point `B = [1, 0.25]` is done geometrically by chaining the arrows: the resulting location is the vector representing the sum (figure 2.8). Adding `B` to `A` thus represents copying point A to a new location — the sentence continues on p.60, where the displacement is described by `B` and the idea is extended to translating whole objects.

paragraphs.excerpt: Reshaping a tensor means rearranging its rows and columns to match a target shape.
paragraphs.what_it_says: Reshaping rearranges a tensor's rows and columns into a target shape; the total number of coefficients is unchanged. The authors illustrate with a (3, 2) matrix reshaped to (6, 1) and then to (2, 3).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The values 0–5 keep their order (read row by row) and are simply re-cut into rows of different length: 3 rows of 2 → 6 rows of 1 → 2 rows of 3. The products 3·2 = 6·1 = 2·3 = 6 show the invariant.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is exactly what `train_images.reshape((60000, 28 * 28))` on p.58 did: each 28 × 28 block of 784 pixels became one row. Any reshape you write must satisfy the same count rule, otherwise NumPy raises an error.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: NumPy fills the new shape in row-major (C) order — last axis fastest — which is why `[[0, 1], [2, 3], [4, 5]]` becomes `[[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]` and not `[[0, 2, 4], [1, 3, 5]]`.

paragraphs.excerpt: A special case of reshaping that’s commonly encountered is transposition. Transposing a
paragraphs.what_it_says: Transposition exchanges a matrix's rows and columns, so row `x[i, :]` becomes column `x[:, i]`. Example: a (300, 20) zero matrix transposed has shape (20, 300).
paragraphs.what_it_means: The entry at position (i, j) moves to (j, i). The shape tuple is reversed. Unlike a plain reshape, which keeps the row-major reading order of the values, transposition reorders them — the authors call it a special case of reshaping in the broad sense of 'rearranging rows and columns'.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: Transposes appear whenever a matrix is oriented the wrong way for a product — e.g. turning a (features, samples) layout into (samples, features) — and in the gradient formulas of later chapters.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: `np.transpose(x)` is also written `x.T`; for a (300, 20) array it returns a view with swapped strides, so no data is copied. For rank > 2 tensors, `np.transpose` can take an `axes` argument to permute any axes.

terminology.meaning: Swapping the rows and columns of a matrix: (x^T)[i, j] = x[j, i].

p.57: matrix products require x.shape[1] == y.shape[0]; transposing is a common way to meet that condition.

paragraphs.excerpt: Because the contents of the tensors manipulated by tensor operations can be interpreted
paragraphs.what_it_says: Since the numbers in a tensor can be read as coordinates of points in a geometric space, every tensor operation has a geometric interpretation. Addition is the first case, starting from the vector `A = [0.5, 1]`.
paragraphs.what_it_means: A rank-1 tensor with two entries is a location in the plane; a tensor with n entries is a point in n-dimensional space. Operations on the numbers therefore move, stretch or rotate points.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This reframing is the foundation of the book's explanation of deep learning: a network is a chain of geometric transformations that untangles data (p.62). Everything from Dense layers to attention can be read this way.

terminology.meaning: Reading tensor values as coordinates so that tensor operations become spatial transformations.

connections: p.62: a neural network as a very complex geometric transformation in high-dimensional space.
p.82: chapter summary — tensor operations encode geometric transformations.

paragraphs.excerpt: It’s a point in a 2D space (see figure 2.6). It’s common to picture
paragraphs.what_it_says: `A = [0.5, 1]` is a point in 2-D space (figure 2.6); it is also commonly drawn as an arrow from the origin to that point (figure 2.7).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Point and arrow are two pictures of the same vector: the point view emphasises *where*, the arrow view emphasises *displacement* (direction and length). The arrow view is what makes addition easy to draw.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: The two views are used interchangeably in the following pages: data samples are points, while the vectors added to them (biases, translations) are arrows.

terminology.meaning: Drawing a vector as a directed segment from the origin (0, 0) to the point with the vector's coordinates.

paragraphs.what_it_says: Adding a second point `B = [1, 0.25]` to `A` is done geometrically by chaining the arrows head to tail; the end of the chain is the vector for the sum (figure 2.8). Adding `B` to `A` represents copying point A to a new location (sentence continues on p.60).
paragraphs.what_it_means: Numerically, `A + B = [0.5 + 1, 1 + 0.25] = [1.5, 1.25]` — the element-wise addition of p.53. Geometrically, start at A and walk along B: you land at (1.5, 1.25). The sum is 'A displaced by B'.
paragraphs.why_it_matters: This is the geometric meaning of the `+ b` in a Dense layer: the bias shifts every point by the same displacement. On p.60 the authors call this a translation and extend it from a single point to an entire object.
paragraphs.technical_idea: Beyond the book: vector addition is commutative, so chaining A then B or B then A ends at the same point — the two paths form a parallelogram.

terminology.meaning: Placing the tail of the second arrow at the head of the first; the sum runs from the origin to the second head.

concepts.name: Tensor reshaping
concepts.definition: Rearranging a tensor's rows and columns to match a target shape, keeping the same total number of coefficients.
concepts.intuition: Pouring the same six numbers into containers of a different layout: 3 × 2, 6 × 1, 2 × 3.
concepts.technical: `x.reshape(new_shape)`; requires prod(new_shape) == prod(x.shape). Values are taken in row-major order and refilled in row-major order (beyond the book).
concepts.significance: Used to flatten images for Dense layers (p.58) and generally to match data layouts to what layers expect.
concepts.misconception: That reshape can change the number of elements or that it transposes. It only re-cuts the same ordered values.

concepts.name: Transposition
concepts.definition: Exchanging the rows and columns of a matrix so that x[i, :] becomes x[:, i]; the shape (m, n) becomes (n, m).
concepts.intuition: Flip the matrix over its main diagonal.
concepts.technical: `np.transpose(x)` (or `x.T`); (x^T)[i, j] = x[j, i]. The book presents it as a special case of reshaping.
concepts.significance: Reorients matrices to satisfy product-compatibility rules; appears throughout gradient computations later in the book.
concepts.misconception: That transpose and reshape((n, m)) give the same result. Both yield shape (n, m), but reshape keeps row-major order whereas transpose swaps the axes, so the element arrangement differs.

concepts.name: Geometric interpretation of tensor operations
concepts.definition: Reading a tensor's contents as the coordinates of points in a geometric space, so that every tensor operation becomes a geometric transformation.
concepts.intuition: Numbers are positions; operations are movements.
concepts.technical: A 2-vector is a point in the plane or an arrow from the origin; adding vectors chains arrows; more operations (translation, rotation, scaling, affine) follow on p.60–61.
concepts.significance: It is the book's central way to understand what a neural network does: a chain of simple geometric transformations in high-dimensional space (p.62).
concepts.misconception: That the geometric view only works in 2-D or 3-D. It is used precisely because it extends to the high-dimensional spaces of real data, even if we can only draw low-dimensional cases.

concepts.name: Vector addition as chaining arrows
concepts.definition: The sum of two vectors is found by placing the second arrow's tail at the first arrow's head; the sum runs from the origin to the final head.
concepts.intuition: Walk along A, then along B; your final position is A + B.
concepts.technical: Coordinate-wise: (A + B)_i = A_i + B_i — the element-wise addition of p.53.
concepts.significance: Adding a vector B to a point A copies A to a new location; applied to many points, this is a translation (p.60).
concepts.misconception: That the sum's length is the sum of the lengths. Only true when the arrows point the same way; generally the chained path is shorter than that.

math.title: Reshaping preserves the number of coefficients
math.source_text: the reshaped tensor has the same total number of coefficients as the initial tensor

variables.meaning: Sizes along each axis of the original shape, e.g. (3, 2).
Sizes along each axis of the target shape, e.g. (6, 1) or (2, 3).

math.operations: Multiply the entries of each shape tuple; the products must be equal.
math.purpose: The feasibility condition for any reshape.
math.interpretation: Reshaping is a relabelling of positions, not a change of data.
math.intuition: Six eggs fit in a 3 × 2, 6 × 1 or 2 × 3 carton, but never a 4 × 2 one.

math.title: Transposition
math.source_text: Transposing a matrix means exchanging its rows and its columns, so that x[i, :] becomes x[:, i]

variables.meaning: A matrix with shape (m, n); here (300, 20).
Row and column indices, which swap roles.

math.operations: Move each entry from (i, j) to (j, i).
math.purpose: Reorients a matrix; a special case of rearranging rows and columns.
math.interpretation: Row i of x is column i of x^T.
math.intuition: Reflect the grid across its top-left-to-bottom-right diagonal.
math.numerical_example: $x = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 3 \\ 4 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ (3 × 2) → $x^{\mathsf T} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 2 & 4 \\ 1 & 3 & 5 \end{pmatrix}$ (2 × 3). Compare with `x.reshape((2, 3))` = [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]: same shape, different arrangement.

math.title: Vector addition in coordinates
math.source_text: A = [0.5, 1]; B = [1, 0.25]; adding B to A by chaining together the vector arrows

variables.meaning: The vector added to A, coordinates (1, 0.25).
The point reached by chaining the arrows, coordinates (1.5, 1.25).

math.operations: Add x-coordinates and y-coordinates separately (element-wise addition).
math.purpose: Gives the numerical counterpart of figure 2.8's chained arrows.
math.interpretation: A + B is point A copied to a new location displaced by B.
math.intuition: Walk 0.5 right and 1 up (A), then 1 right and 0.25 up (B): you end at (1.5, 1.25).
math.numerical_example: Order does not matter: B + A = (1 + 0.5, 0.25 + 1) = (1.5, 1.25) as well — the two routes close a parallelogram (my addition, not in the book).

deeper.title: Reshape versus transpose on the same six numbers
deeper.body:
Beyond the book: both operations can take a (3, 2) matrix to shape (2, 3), but they are not the same.

| operation | result |
|---|---|
| `x.reshape((2, 3))` | `[[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]` — row-major order preserved |
| `np.transpose(x)` | `[[0, 2, 4], [1, 3, 5]]` — row i becomes column i |

The book calls transposition a 'special case of reshaping' in the sense of rearranging rows and columns; in NumPy terms it is an axis permutation rather than a `reshape` call. Keep the distinction in mind when fixing shape errors: a `reshape` that merely makes shapes match can silently scramble your data if what you actually needed was a transpose.

deeper.title: Chaining arrows, step by step
deeper.body:
1. Draw A: an arrow from (0, 0) to (0.5, 1).
2. Draw B *starting at the head of A*: from (0.5, 1), move 1 right and 0.25 up, arriving at (1.5, 1.25).
3. The sum A + B is the arrow from the origin straight to (1.5, 1.25).
4. Check with coordinates: (0.5 + 1, 1 + 0.25) = (1.5, 1.25) — identical to element-wise addition (p.53).
5. Read the result as the book does: point A has been *copied* to a new location; the displacement is B.

deeper.title: From one point to a whole batch
deeper.body: Combine this page with broadcasting (p.55): if `X` holds 32 points as rows and `b` is a 2-vector, `X + b` moves every point by the same arrow b. That is what the `+ b` of a Dense layer does to a batch of samples, and it is what p.60 will call translating an object. The geometric reading of addition therefore applies not only to one vector A but to the entire data set at once. (My synthesis of p.55, this page and the next.)

deeper.title: Directions on a map
deeper.body: A vector as a point is a pin on a map: 'you are at (0.5, 1)'. A vector as an arrow is a set of directions: 'go 0.5 east and 1 north'. Adding B = [1, 0.25] is following a second set of directions from where the first left you. Whether you think of the result as a new pin (point view) or as the combined directions from home (arrow view), you end up at (1.5, 1.25).

misconceptions.claim: Geometric interpretation is a loose metaphor that applies only to 2-D examples.
misconceptions.correction: The authors state that because tensor contents are coordinates, all tensor operations have a geometric interpretation; 2-D is just what can be drawn.
